entries.title: Swiss glaciers lose of more than 5% in ice volume in 2026
entries.summary: Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next 10-15 years.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next 10-15 years.

Glaciers in Switzerland have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts said Thursday.

The experts said Swiss glaciers are melting rapidly and this year saw the second-biggest drop on record due to unprecedented heat waves in Europe.

There was a drop of 5.5% of Swiss glaciers this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study.

GLAMOS warns of total glacier loss

According to the report, over the past five years, the Swiss glaciers have lost almost ​a fifth of their ice, warning that in the future it could threaten water supplies.

The report also raised questions about the long-term survival of Europe's ice fields.

"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice."

Little winter snowfall and record summer temperatures led Huss to call 2026 "a catastrophic year."

"This is a glacier that isn't surviving," he said. "There will probably be no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years."

The GLAMOS report reiterates concerns about the impact of global warming, especially in Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," Huss said, using the term for climate change caused by human activity. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

entries.title: US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says
entries.summary: The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.
entries.content:
United States of America

US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says

October 1, 2026

The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States military has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%.

He made the announcement while addressing junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia during what he called his "State of the Force" address.

"The number-crunchers say we fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth said, adding: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%."

"So yes, 20% reduction across the board," he noted. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."

Cutting the fat or a purge?

The address came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.

Since the start of Donald Trump's second term as president early last year, a number of top military personnel have been forced out of their positions.

Trump, for instance, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Charles "CQ" Brown, without explanation in February 2025.

Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, and a Navy admiral assigned to NATO.

Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the military leaders he wants.

But Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the US military.

Some members of Congress have called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly told the Associated Press. Kelly is a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."

Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning.

"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.

What Hegseth said about the new command

On Wednesday, Hegseth also announced his intention to create a new drone-focused warfare command, which would oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities.

He said that "the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."

The defense secretary pointed to Ukraine's use of drones to combat Russian forces to underscore how warfare and battlefield tactics are changing.

"Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt," Hegseth said.

To study the future of warfare, the secretary unveiled a task force led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.

He said the work "will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." The Pentagon chief pointed to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

entries.title: France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate
entries.summary: Student protests have grown in scale and intensity, with violent clashes in some places leading to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries.
entries.content:
France

France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate

October 1, 2026

Student protests have grown in scale and intensity, with violent clashes in some places leading to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries.

Security forces in France on Wednesday detained over 600 people as protests at high schools in parts of the country have intensified.   

Authorities said violent clashes and arson attacks have also left dozens of security personnel wounded.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he called an "escalation of violence" outside certain schools.

The violence left 83 police officers and gendarmes wounded on Wednesday, he said, adding that 32 teachers and pupils were also injured. The protests affected 356 schools, the minister noted.

He slammed the "targeting of law enforcement officers, the throwing of projectiles, acts of violence, verbal abuse, attempted arson, and what amounts... to urban violence."

Why are students protesting?

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week.

They are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages.

"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather.

The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions.

The cities worst affected Wednesday include Paris, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lyon in the southeast, and the northern city of Lille, where police again used tear gas in clashes, the AFP news agency reported.

What did the government say?

President Emmanuel Macron said the young people's concerns were legitimate but could in no way justify violence and attacks on police officers and teachers, among others.

"High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash ⁠cans set on fire," he told reporters in Madrid.

Both Macron and Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence during the protests.

"We observed that, in certain places, ⁠there were ​individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir ​up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," Nunez said.

Over the past few days, officials and politicians have denounced the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger.

On Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."

"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Gaza: NGO reports dire camp conditions, says Israel is moving 'Yellow Line'
entries.summary: The Danish Refugee Council alleges that Israel is employing "a policy of protracted displacement" in Gaza. It says the so-called "Yellow Line" is creeping west toward the coast, preventing many from returning home.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Gaza: NGO reports moving 'Yellow Line,' dire camp conditions

October 1, 2026

The Danish Refugee Council alleges that Israel is employing "a policy of protracted displacement" in Gaza. It says the so-called "Yellow Line" is creeping west toward the coast, preventing many from returning home.

A new report on conditions in the Gaza Strip says that the roughly 1.8 million Palestinians in Gaza, or 86% of the population, living in displacement sites often face inhumane living conditions. 

The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) published its findings on Thursday, almost three years after the October 7 terror attacks against Israel that triggered the war in Gaza, and a year after the phased October 10 ceasefire plan that was supposed to usher in the war's end.

"The October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza was supposed to end civilians' suffering. Nearly a year on, it exists largely in name only. Displacement in Gaza has not ended; it has changed shape," the report says.

The findings are based on group discussions with 195 people living in internal displacement camps across five governorates in Gaza.

What did the DRC say about the Yellow Line?

Entitled "Confined by Design: The Human Cost of Protracted Displacement in Gaza," the report accuses Israel of "a policy of protracted displacement" since the ceasefire deal was reached. 

One means of ensuring this, the DRC says, is the so-called "Yellow Line," which demarcates the area of eastern Gaza near the border that is controlled by the Israeli military and is, according to the report, creeping toward the coast.

"In addition to protracted displacement for hundreds of thousands of people, the defining feature of the so-called ceasefire is the Yellow Line which continues expanding westward and swallowing up more land, effectively squeezing families into 30% of Gaza's territory," said the NGO's country director for the occupied Palestinian territories, Alan Moseley.

Other groups, including the UN, have also reported the westward movement of the Yellow Line, as has the Israeli government, although some details differ.

Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put the share of Gaza's territory inside the Yellow Line at 60% rather than 70%, but he also said the plan was to expand the area. 

The DRC report also said aid organizations "describe being unable to operate within several kilometers of the line, either due to access constraints or security concerns."

It said that this led to crucial aid and supplies failing to reach displacement camps nearer the boundary.

What did the report say about living conditions in displacement camps?

The DRC and the Agricultural Development Association (PARC) highlighted a series of major shortcomings in the often informal tent shelters and makeshift camps that have sprung up amid Gaza's rubble, where more than eight in 10 residents are believed to be living.

These included but were not limited to:

  • 80% of respondents reporting shortages of water both for washing and drinking
  • Displaced households relying on outdoor cesspits
  • Multiple families sharing single latrines, increasing the risk of gender-based violence and abuse
  • Rat and rodent infestations exacerbated by the unsanitary conditions
  • Food scarcity and lacking infrastructure for cooking, increasing risks of burns or injury preparing meals
  • Rapid localized spread of illnesses and infections. For instance, more than 4,000 chickenpox cases were recorded in Khan Younis displacement camps in July alone
  • Lacking and overburdened medical facilities with only half of hospitals and just over a third of primary healthcare centers still operational
  • Lacking or non-existent formal education provision for young people, now lasting almost three years in some cases
  • Reports of security concerns, particularly among men, because of the continued presence of artillery strikes, drones and stray gunfire
  • Safety risks posed by unexploded and undiscovered ordnance, particularly when trying to clear rubble or return to areas where people originally lived

The Danish Refugee Council also laid particular emphasis on lacking site management mechanisms at displacement camps.

It said only 36% of sites currently had a designated site manager, typically a national NGO, coordinating services and managing conditions.

Sites with such partners "have a structured community channel through which a gap, such as a collapsing cesspit, a missing water delivery, or an unsafe walkway, can be identified, escalated, and resolved," the report said.

Israel has not yet commented on the newly released report.

What actions did the DRC recommend?

The DRC and PARC issued a number of appeals and recommendations, some to "all parties to the conflict," most to "the Government of Israel, as the occupying power of Gaza" and others to "the international community" and "donors and humanitarian actors."

These included:

  • Completely upholding pledges to cease hostilities
  • Ending attacks against civilians, humanitarian workers and medical personnel
  • Guaranteeing humanitarian access and medical evacuation pathways
  • Supporting the establishment of a UN mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations.

The groups called on Israel to "halt the further expansion of the Yellow Line" and to "disclose its current and future route transparently."

They also urged Israel to cease the construction of permanent military infrastructure in the area and to provide "credible assurance that current troop positions are not intended to be permanent."

They appealed for fewer restrictions on aid access, particularly so-called "dual-use" restrictions affecting medical supplies, water, sanitation and hygiene items, pest control, rubble removal and fuel.

The report also warned that political and donor interest in the situation had declined markedly in the year since the ceasefire, even though conditions had not improved proportionately.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
entries.summary: Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are moving forward with plans to establish deportation centers outside the EU. An African partner country has reportedly already been selected.
entries.content:
Europe

EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027

September 30, 2026

Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are moving forward with plans to establish deportation centers outside the EU. An African partner country has reportedly already been selected.

Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles.

During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called "return hubs" is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency. 

Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda, but neither country has been confirmed as the location.

No sealed detention centers

"We are not talking about centers in the sense that someone whose asylum application is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country," Plevris said.

The plan was rather to establish "open facilities" while the final return to the actual country of origin is being organized, he added.

The responsibility for the transferred individuals will not be transferred to the African partner country in order to prevent legal action for human rights violations, but will remain with the five participating EU member states. The EU "group of five" will also finance the project entirely on its own.

There are also plans for international organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to monitor operations to ensure that international human rights standards and principles of international law are upheld.

Various attempts have been made in recent years to outsource asylum proceedings or deportations to countries outside the EU. None of these models worked as planned. All failed due to legal impediments, changes in government, or high costs. Below are some of the best-known precedents.

The British "Rwanda Model" (2022–2024)

The United Kingdom, under the Conservative government of Boris Johnson — and later under Rishi Sunak — sought to permanently deport migrants who had entered the country irregularly via the English Channel to Rwanda so they could undergo their asylum proceedings there.

However, the British Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal, finding that there were substantial grounds for believing that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned to countries where they could face persecution or other inhumane treatment.

Prior to that, the British government had spent £715 million (€835 million/$966 million) in taxpayer funds on the Rwanda partnership and related implementation costs. In return, a total of four people had voluntarily relocated to Rwanda

Italy's Albania model (in place since 2024)

Under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italy signed an agreement with Albania to transport migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean directly to Italian-run centers established in Albania where expedited asylum proceedings could be conducted.

However, immediately after the camps opened, Italian courts halted the relocation. Judges argued that countries of origin such as Bangladesh or Egypt should not be classified as "safe" outright if certain groups face persecution there. These first migrants had to be returned to Italy immediately.

Italy is now using one of the camps solely as a deportation center for men whose asylum applications in Italy have been definitively rejected. Since the facility was converted in March 2025, only about 500 people have been sent there. By 2028, this comes at an estimated total cost of more than €670 million ($775 million).

Denmark's stand-alone initiatives (2021–2023)

In 2021, Denmark passed a law intended to allow asylum seekers to be flown to third countries outside the EU. Copenhagen engaged in intensive negotiations with Rwanda regarding a dedicated reception center. However, the European Commission and human rights organizations sharply criticized the initiative. In early 2023, the Danish government put the negotiations with Rwanda on hold. It became clear that the Danish plan was virtually impossible to implement legally and logistically. The government subsequently moved toward pursuing third-country return arrangements in cooperation with other European countries.

Changing legal framework

According to previous EU law, deportations to third countries often failed as courts required that a migrant have a personal connection to that third country, whether through language skills, relatives living there or a previous stay. The revised European asylum law, however, now allows individuals required to leave the EU to be transferred to a safe third country without a prior personal connection in certain circumstances — provided there is a corresponding agreement or arrangement with the third country. 

A further basis for this new joint effort is the EU Return Regulation, agreed upon politically on June 17, 2026 by the Council and European Parliament. However, the regulation has not yet been formally adopted by the Council. Unlike before, the new legislation is an EU regulation and no longer merely a directive. As a result, it will apply directly once it enters into force in the EU member states bound by it. The regulation thus establishes a common EU framework for such return centers.

Furthermore, according to the new plans, the entire asylum procedure will no longer be outsourced to non-EU countries. The United Kingdom and Italy rejected this proposal. Instead, these "return hubs" will serve solely as transit stations for individuals whose asylum applications have already been legally rejected while they are financed and monitored by EU member states.

Inadequate oversight and high costs?

Supporters hope that these measures will undermine the basis for human rights lawsuits regarding permanent asylum protection. Critics such as Doctors Without Borders and Amnesty International still see significant risks: They doubt that independent oversight, effective legal representation and medical care can be fully guaranteed in the hubs. They also fear that third countries could still deport people to their unsafe home countries without proper assessment.

Furthermore, experience to date shows that the construction and security of such centers, as well as the transport of those affected, often costs hundreds of millions of euro, and only a small number of people actually end up being returned.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
entries.summary: A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after the copilot stabbed the captain. Eyewitnesses said he attempted to crash the plane before he was subdued by passengers.
entries.content:
Israel

Flydubai pilot stabbed in attempt to down Israel-bound plane

Published September 30, 2026last updated September 30, 2026

A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after the copilot stabbed the captain. Eyewitnesses said he attempted to crash the plane before he was subdued by passengers.

An Indian pilot was stabbed by his copilot on Wednesday in a failed attempt to crash a Flydubai plane that was bound for Israel.

After he was stabbed, Captain Smit Machchhar opened the cockpit in time for other passengers to intervene, and the plane was ultimately able to land safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, said that "an attempted jihadist terror attack" had been thwarted after several passengers subdued the copilot.

Flydubai confirmed that all passengers were safe. It later announced it had suspended flights to and from Israel amid an ongoing investigation.

Too early to say who's behind the plot, says Netanyahu

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and non-Israeli carriers following the Flydubai flight incident.

In an interview to ‌Fox News host Sean Hannity on the ​network's "Hannity" ⁠program later on Wednesday, Netanyahu said it was too early to say who was behind the ‌foiled ⁠bid ⁠to crash the flight.

He added that Israel would "possibly" be ​participating in the probe into the ​incident.

"It's ‌too early to say, the attacking pilot is ... now being investigated ‌in Saudi Arabia. I ‌think ​he'll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least ​where he left, where he flew off from, and we'll ⁠be ​following and possibly ​also participating in this investigation," the Israeli premier said.

His comment came in response to a ⁠question ​about whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement in the incident.

Passengers return to Israel

On Wednesday evening, passengers from the diverted Flydubai flight arrived in Israel on a replacement plane, where numerous relatives were waiting for them.

Netanyahu also met with some of the passengers. A video posted to Netanyahu's X account showed him at the Tel Aviv airport meeting a man called Yaniv Hayoun, who still had blood on his shirt after the midflight altercation.

The video described Yaniv as one of the passengers who entered the aircraft's cockpit.

Later, Netanyahu named the Indian pilot who was injured in an altercation with his co-pilot, who allegedly attempted to crash the Flydubai flight.

"My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery. Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on social media.

"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."

The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar is in stable condition and is being treated in a Tabuk hospital after an emergency landing.

In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi also lauded Machchhar, calling him a "hero."

"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, ​he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," Modi said.

Meanwhile, the Israeli foreign minister said that he spoke with his UAE counterpart Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

"Mutual determination was expressed to strengthen relations between the countries on all levels and to collaborate against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region," Saar wrote on X.

Saar also spoke with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul over the phone.

Wadephul said that he strongly condemned the incident as a serious attack on civil aviation. He added that his thoughts were with those who survived the flight and with those who feared for the lives of their loved ones. Wadephul also said that the circumstances surrounding the incident must be clarified quickly and thoroughly.

Later, US President Donald Trump announced he had discussed the Flydubai flight incident with Netanyahu. Trump said Netanyahu told him an Israeli plumber had helped prevent the aircraft from crashing.

"I did speak to Bibi Netanyahu at length about this event, and it seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot," Trump told reporters.

What happened on the Flydubai flight?

Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.

"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.

Later, a Flydubai spokesperson said that the reasons for an altercation that "occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073" remained unknown and were under formal investigation.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," a spokesperson said in a statement published by the AFP news agency.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 initially showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, diverting back toward Dubai. It later showed the aircraft continuing toward Tel Aviv. There was no immediate explanation for the change.

How far did the plane fall?

The Israeli news portal Ynet reported that the aircraft entered a steep descent and that passengers helped one pilot prevent the other from crashing the plane.

Flight tracking data shows the aircraft suddenly losing around half its altitude as it neared Saudi Arabia's border with Jordan.

The plane dropped from nearly 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) at 05:21 GMT/UTC to below 17,000 feet (5,180 meters) at 05:22 GMT/UTC, according to Flightradar data.

Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military scrambled fighter jets amid initial fears of a possible hijacking. That possibility was later dismissed, according to the reports.

Israeli minister says 'attempted jihadist terror attack' thwarted

Israeli leaders announced that a "jihadist" pilot had attempted to crash a Flydubai plane carrying mostly Israeli passengers.

In a video message, Netanyahu said that "during the flight... one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board."

He added that passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where the pilot was arrested.

"I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster," Netanyahu said.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was "thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers."

Earlier, Netanyahu's office said he had held consultations over the incident and was monitoring developments.

"The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel," his office said.

An unnamed senior Israeli government official told Channel 12 that a major disaster had been averted.

Meanwhile, Israel's Foreign Ministry informed its diplomats that the incident was "an attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords."

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Zac Crellin, Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: France's Macron, Spain's Sanchez welcome idea of UK rejoining EU after Burnham remarks
entries.summary: During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out rejoining the bloc.
entries.content:
Europe

France, Spain welcome idea of UK rejoining EU

September 30, 2026

During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out rejoining the bloc.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday welcomed the idea of the United Kingdom rejoining the European Union. 

During a visit to Madrid while meeting with Sanchez, Macron reacted to the idea of a UK rejoin with two words in English: "Welcome back."

"If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news both for his country and for Europeans," Macron continued in French.

At the same time, Macron said the UK cannot take an a la carte approach to its relationship with the EU, while remaining outside the bloc.

"You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union and decide to take what suits us and not the rest," he said.

Sanchez said the UK's decision to leave the EU as a result of a referendum in 2016 is "a huge loss, both for the British population and for the whole European project."

The Spanish prime minister said if the UK indeed does try to rejoin the EU, "then of course Spain would applaud it and open its arms again to a brotherly people."

In a separate statement from the EU, European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said: "The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward."

"We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward," Ujvari said.

Burnham: UK should consider options in regards to EU ties

In an interview with the BBC earlier on Wednesday, UK Prime Minister  Andy Burnham said Britain should look at various options when it comes to the relationship with the EU.

"We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," Burnham said, while saying one option would be to "go all the way."

Other possibilities might include rejoining the EU's single market or a customs union between the two sides, he said.

During a speech at the annual Labour Party conference on Tuesday, Burnham said that "Brexit has done more harm than good." He added he would set out "different options" for the UK-EU relationship closer to a summit between the two sides in November.

Such a decision to move closer or rejoin the EU could open up a tense political debate in the UK.

Although recent public surveys suggest that the majority of Britons back rejoining, the idea of adopting the Euro currency or contributing to the EU budget would likely spark fierce backlash. Moreover, the UK is unlikely to receive the same exemptions it had when it was previously a member of the EU.

For now, Burnham is committed to the 2024 Labour Party manifesto, which ruled out rejoining the EU and other elements such as returning to the EU single market. However, Burnham could push Labour for a closer approach to the EU in the next general election, which is slated for no later than August 2029.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?
entries.summary: It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants open conflict with Iran.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?

September 30, 2026

It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants open conflict with Iran.

Last week, some students in Saudi Arabia were told they should stay at home and attend classes online, due to continued threats from attacks by the Houthi group in neighboring Yemen. But the very next day, they were given the all-clear and allowed to return to school in person.

The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen seems to have become part of everyday life in Saudi Arabia. After a period of comparative calm, the Houthis have been ramping up attacks on the country, starting July, and have fired many missiles and drones over the border.

Over recent weeks, the Houthi militia have also pushed further into Yemen, taking more control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea. This means they can oversee maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The renewed Houthi attacks endanger Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's ambitious project to move the kingdom away from its dependence on oil revenues, which was conceived by Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. To make Vision 2030 a reality, Saudi Arabia needs stability — but right now, the outlook is moving in the opposite direction.

"The escalation in Yemen is drawing the Saudis deeper into the regional war, a war that Saudi Arabia actually wanted to prevent," said Marcus Schneider, who heads the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Peace and Security Project in the Middle East.

Impact on world's energy

Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to Houthi attacks, which have already disrupted the so-called East-West pipeline, which runs for over 1,200 kilometers. It was being used to transport oil after other routes, such as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, became precarious due to fighting between the United States, Israel and Iran.

Houthi attacks disabled the pipeline although reports from a week ago suggest it is being used again. And thanks to the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which means "gate of tears" in English — is also coming under pressure.

Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in the Middle East program of the US think tank, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, calls it a "one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures." In fact, it may send the Saudis back to the Strait of Hormuz to try to ship their oil, even though that route is still heavily restricted.

Who will help?

It is unlikely that Saudi ally, the US, is going to send help. Washington has said it will support the Saudis with intelligence and reconnaissance, but President Donald Trump appears reluctant to get involved in a direct military campaign against the Houthis.

According to a US-based think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, this may partially be because the it is feeling the strain of its ongoing campaign against Iran.

"The US military is reportedly facing serious challenges, including shortages of some sophisticated interceptors," the CSIS wrote in a commentary last week.

The US Council on Foreign Relations, or CFR, has also written about dwindling stocks of Patriot and interceptor missiles, as well as cruise missiles.

So the risk of opening another front in its war with Iran, in Yemen, is not a welcome prospect for the US.

As it is, US airstrikes are unlikely to resolve the Houthi problem anyway. The CFR writes that to defuse the Houthi threat, a large, coordinated ground operation is needed, especially if forces want to push the Yemeni militia back out of the areas they recently took around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia is not too enthusiastic about this either. Despite help from the US and neighboring United Arab Emirates, a Saudi coalition that fought against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022 failed to achieve any kind of decisive victory. It also demonstrated the limits of Saudi military power.

There's clear military asymmetry. Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. But the Houthis don't need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to use missiles and drones to threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping.

"The Houthis are well-established in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows," Schneider told DW. "Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, needs stability above all for its 2030 economic vision. And this is currently further away than ever."

Help from the Europeans?

Since early 2024, through what is known as Operation Aspides, Europe has been protecting international shipping in the Red Sea. Italy has recently said it intends to secure passage for its own merchant ships with its navy. And a few days ago France said it would send soldiers, radar systems and air defense to the Saudis in order to protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the terminus of the East-West pipeline.

Still, these European initiatives are unlikely to bring about any sort of strategic shift in Yemen. And experts argue Europe is unwilling to accept the political and military cost of a protracted war there.

"The fact that France has now announced it will provide concrete military assistance has been received very positively in Riyadh," Schneider explained. "But still the question remains as to whether this can fundamentally alter the military balance."

The recently formed mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, known as the Mecca alliance, also has its limits. The military leaders of all three countries have consulted with one another over recent Houthis attacks but Turkey and Pakistan are also reluctant to be drawn into a conflict that would see them confronting Iran directly.

Diplomacy the way forward

All this means that diplomatic overtures will likely become more important again.

In a previous interview with DW, Abdulghani al-Iryani of the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies noted that the Houthis do actually have an interest in relations with Saudi Arabia.

"Yemen is completely economically dependent on Saudi Arabia, both as a source of humanitarian aid and as a labor market for Yemeni migrant workers," al-Iryani said.

In recent years, Saudi Arabia has tried to curb the Houthis' influence through diplomacy and by uniting divided Yemeni government forces. However the militia's current advance seems to demonstrate the limitations of this strategy.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
entries.summary: The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?
entries.content:
Germany

Do Jewish representatives see the Left Party as antisemitic?

September 30, 2026

The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?

The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election on September 20. This means there's a good chance that the party's top candidate, Elif Eralp, could become Berlin's next mayor — making her the first member of the Left Party to hold that office.

Preliminary talks with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the environmentalist Green Party are scheduled to take place on October 1. If the talks are successful, it would represent a major step toward forming a coalition government.

Securing a clear commitment from the Left Party against antisemitism within its own ranks is seen as a prerequisite for successful cooperation. Yet doubts still persist about whether the party and its representatives can adequately protect Jewish life in the city.

During the election campaign, a performance at a Left Party event by the rapper Dahabflex made headlines and sparked outrage when he used slogans seen as antisemitic during his performance. And later, at an event held by the Left Party to celebrate its election victory, an appearance was made by Ibrahim Ibrahim — a supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is on the EU's list of terrorist organizations. The leaders of the Left Party have repeatedly distanced themselves from both incidents, both at the federal and state levels.

The Central Council of Jews in Germany is warning

However, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, thinks these statements are mere lip service.

"In the fight against antisemitism, which is tolerated and allowed to run rampant within the party's ranks, the Left Party no longer has any credibility," reads a press statement released two days after the election. Schuster explicitly appealed to the SPD and the Greens not to form a coalition with the election winner.

High-ranking members of the federal government have also spoken out. Wolfram Weimer, government commissioner for culture and media who has no party affiliation, accused the Left Party of "openly flaunting antisemitism" and called into question the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in funding for the capital's cultural sector for the coming decade — a deal that had already been agreed upon with the Berlin state government. Weimer claimed that many figures in the cultural sector are alarmed by the prospect of a government led by the Left Party.

'Antisemitism and expropriations threaten the economy'

Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also voiced concern. A video titled "Antisemitism and Expropriations Threaten the Economy" is available on her ministry's Instagram account, in reference also to the Left Party's plans to nationalize large private housing companies.

Reiche describes the Left as a party "that openly embraces antisemitism, that instills fear in the Jews of this city, that opposes Jewish life and that cheerfully welcomes organized crime at election parties."

The Left Party is now seeking an injunction to compel the Minister of Economic Affairs to delete the video.

"Reiche is using taxpayer money to spread propaganda against the Left Party on the Economy Ministry's official channel," said Left Party Federal Co-Chair Ines Schwerdtner.

150 prominent Jews come to the defense of the Left Party

In an open letter, a group of 150 prominent Jews from various social backgrounds has voiced support for the Left Party. Among those who signed it are the author Eva Menasse and the former director of the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Susan Neiman. They advocate for a "social and safe city" and emphasize the importance of voting for different parties.

They explain their motivation as follows: "We are writing this letter because, over the past few weeks, we have heard the same claim time and again: that the Left is dangerous for Jews, and that a coalition involving the party poses a danger to our safety. We reject this claim not because we downplay concerns about our safety, but because we actually take them seriously."

Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."

In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."

The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.

Elif Eralp wants to build bridges

Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.

The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.

"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."

With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.

"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.

Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.

One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.

"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."

Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
entries.summary: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.

Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.

"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.

"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.

Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.

"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."

Senegal an attractive option for many reasons

The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.

"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.

Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.

"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.

"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."

From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold
